verses.text: In those days the crowd once again became very large, and they had nothing to eat. Jesus called the disciples to Him and said,
"I have compassion for this crowd, because they have already been with Me three days and have nothing to eat.
If I send them home hungry, they will faint along the way. For some of them have come a great distance."
His disciples replied, "Where in this desolate place could anyone find enough bread to feed all these people?"
"How many loaves do you have?" Jesus asked. "Seven," they replied.

And He instructed the crowd to sit down on the ground. Then He took the seven loaves, gave thanks and broke them, and gave them to His disciples to set before the people. And they distributed them to the crowd.
They also had a few small fish, and Jesus blessed them and ordered that these be set before them as well.
The people ate and were satisfied, and the disciples picked up seven basketfuls of broken pieces that were left over.
And about four thousand men were present. And when Jesus had dismissed the crowd,
He immediately got into the boat with His disciples and went to the district of Dalmanutha.
Then the Pharisees came and began to argue with Jesus, testing Him by demanding from Him a sign from heaven.
Jesus sighed deeply in His spirit and said, "Why does this generation demand a sign? Truly I tell you, no sign will be given to this generation."
And He left them, got back into the boat, and crossed to the other side.
Now the disciples had forgotten to take bread, except for one loaf they had with them in the boat.
"Watch out!" He cautioned them. "Beware of the leaven of the Pharisees and of Herod."
So they began to discuss with one another the fact that they had no bread.
Aware of their conversation, Jesus asked them, "Why are you debating about having no bread? Do you still not see or understand? Do you have such hard hearts?
'Having eyes, do you not see? And having ears, do you not hear?' And do you not remember?
When I broke the five loaves for the five thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?" "Twelve," they answered.
"And when I broke the seven loaves for the four thousand, how many basketfuls of broken pieces did you collect?" "Seven," they said.
Then He asked them, "Do you still not understand?"
When they arrived at Bethsaida, some people brought a blind man and begged Jesus to touch him.
So He took the blind man by the hand and led him out of the village. Then He spit on the man's eyes and placed His hands on him. "Can you see anything?" He asked.
The man looked up and said, "I can see the people, but they look like trees walking around."
Once again Jesus placed His hands on the man's eyes, and when he opened them his sight was restored, and he could see everything clearly.
Jesus sent him home and said, "Do not go back into the village."
Then Jesus and His disciples went on to the villages around Caesarea Philippi. On the way, He questioned His disciples: "Who do people say I am?"
They replied, "Some say John the Baptist; others say Elijah; and still others, one of the prophets."
"But what about you?" Jesus asked. "Who do you say I am?" Peter answered, "You are the Christ."
And Jesus warned them not to tell anyone about Him.
Then He began to teach them that the Son of Man must suffer many things and be rejected by the elders, chief priests, and scribes, and that He must be killed and after three days rise again.
He spoke this message quite frankly, and Peter took Him aside and began to rebuke Him.
But Jesus, turning and looking at His disciples, rebuked Peter and said, "Get behind Me, Satan! For you do not have in mind the things of God, but the things of men."
Then Jesus called the crowd to Him along with His disciples, and He told them, "If anyone wants to come after Me, he must deny himself and take up his cross and follow Me.
For whoever wants to save his life will lose it, but whoever loses his life for My sake and for the gospel will save it.
What does it profit a man to gain the whole world, yet forfeit his soul?
Or what can a man give in exchange for his soul?
If anyone is ashamed of Me and My words in this adulterous and sinful generation, the Son of Man will also be ashamed of him when He comes in His Father's glory with the holy angels."

context.author: Traditionally John Mark, a companion of Peter
context.genre: Narrative Gospel — a second feeding miracle, a demand for a sign, a warning about corrupting influence, a two-stage healing, and the Gospel's structural turning point
context.audience: Roman Christian readers, watching the disciples' understanding grow only gradually, step by step, mirrored by the unusual two-stage healing at its center
context.setting: This chapter moves through Gentile Decapolis territory (feeding four thousand), Dalmanutha on the western shore, Bethsaida, and finally north to Caesarea Philippi at the base of Mount Hermon — a city built around pagan shrines to the god Pan, a strikingly idol-filled backdrop for Peter's confession that Jesus is the Christ.
context.custom: Rabbis typically taught by citing a chain of earlier authorities behind their interpretation. "Leaven" as a teaching image drew on something every listener understood physically — a small amount works through an entire batch of dough, exactly how Jesus describes corrupting influence spreading quietly through a whole community.
context.timelineImmediate: This chapter is the structural hinge of Mark's whole Gospel — Peter's confession at Caesarea Philippi is followed immediately by Jesus' first direct, explicit prediction of His coming death and resurrection, turning the narrative decisively from Galilean ministry toward the road to Jerusalem.
context.timelineBible: Peter's confession that Jesus is "the Christ" (v.29) directly invokes the royal covenant God made with David in 2 Samuel 7:12-16 — not simply calling Jesus a good teacher, but identifying Him with a centuries-old promise of a coming King.
context.sparkNotes: Jesus feeds four thousand people, refuses the Pharisees' demand for a sign, then heals a blind man in two distinct stages — the only miracle in the Gospels performed this way, mirroring the disciples' own gradual understanding. At Caesarea Philippi, Peter confesses "You are the Christ," and Jesus immediately predicts His coming death for the first time, rebuking Peter sharply when he objects, before calling everyone present to take up their own cross.

translation.meaning: "Anointed One" — the Greek equivalent of the Hebrew "Messiah," God's promised King.

occurrences.note: One of the most common words in the whole New Testament — hundreds of uses across the Gospels, Acts, and every epistle.

translation.meaning: A literal Roman execution instrument, here used as a call to voluntary, daily self-denial — a genuinely shocking image to a first-century audience for whom crucifixion was a real, visible form of state execution.
One's whole life or true self — the same word can mean simply "life" or the deeper, eternal self, and Jesus deliberately plays on both senses in these four verses.

gospelParallels.note: Matthew's parallel account of the feeding of the four thousand.
Matthew's parallel account of Peter's confession, the passion prediction, and the call to take up the cross.
Luke's shorter version of the same sequence of events.

otBackground.note: The Davidic covenant behind the title "Christ" Peter uses in his confession.
"Having eyes, do you not see?" — a phrase Jesus draws directly from this Old Testament pattern of spiritual blindness.
The suffering servant's death as divine necessity — background for Jesus' "must suffer" language in His first passion prediction.

commentary.note: Henry notices Jesus doesn't simply repeat His earlier method: with five loaves He fed five thousand, but rather than reasoning "five fed five thousand, so four should feed four thousand," He takes all seven loaves available this time and uses every bit of them — teaching, in Henry's words, that we should "take things as they are, and accommodate ourselves to them; use what we have, and make the best of that which is."

Henry credits the crowd's devotion directly: many had come from far away and their food had long since run out, "yet they continued with Christ, and did not speak of leaving him till he spoke of dismissing them" — true zeal, he notes, makes nothing of hardship in the pursuit of what it values.

Ryle points to 'the strange mixture of grace and infirmity which may be found in the heart of a true Christian' in Peter's sudden turn — the very man who had just made such a noble confession, moments later presuming to rebuke his own Master for speaking of His coming death.
